extracted.intended_audience: general readers, educators, and self-directed learners interested in reading and education
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on choosing what to read and how to balance humane letters and natural science in general education; guidance aimed at forming disciplined, meaningful reading and curricular habits for the majority of learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution of human nature (four powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we set ourselves to enumerate the powers which go to the building up of human life: the power of conduct, the power of intellect and knowledge, the power of beauty, and the power of social life and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers are not to be treated in isolation; education should 'meet and adjust the claims of them all' so that one attains soberness, righteousness, and wisdom. Use this rough scheme as a guide to what education must serve rather than privileging one power exclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural science vs humane letters: knowledge of things versus relating knowledge to conduct and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science is a 'knowledge of things'—it makes us 'see that' facts happen—whereas humane letters serve to relate knowledge to our sense for conduct and our sense for beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the reality and discipline of natural science (habit of dealing with facts) but insist that science by itself gives knowledge not put into relation with conduct and beauty; that relational work is the province of humane letters. Do not dismiss scientific results; instead use letters to interpret and humanize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about making natural science the chief part of majority education
rubrics_metrics.description: It is proposed by some reformers 'to make the training in natural science the main part of education, for the great majority of mankind,' but the author parts company with that view and urges caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the value of scientific training as a discipline and instrument-knowledge, but consider the 'constitution of human nature' and the generality of mankind's instinct to relate knowledge to conduct and beauty. Reserve full scientific specialization for those with exceptional aptitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The instinct to relate knowledge to conduct and beauty is fundamental
rubrics_metrics.description: Following our instinct for intellect and knowledge, we acquire pieces of knowledge and then 'there arises the desire to relate these pieces of knowledge to our sense for conduct, to our sense for beauty'—and there is 'weariness and dissatisfaction if the desire is balked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design education and reading so they satisfy this instinct: teaching should not only supply isolated facts but show connections to moral and aesthetic life. Recognize that satisfying this instinct is a major source of letters' appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanities (poetry and eloquence) have unique power to engage emotions and relate science to moral/aesthetic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Have poetry and eloquence the power of calling out the emotions?' Experience shows they do, and 'they have the power... of relating the modern results of natural science to man's instinct for conduct, his instinct for beauty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical and best literature and art as instruments to 'fortify,' 'elevate,' 'quicken,' and 'suggest'—helping people integrate modern scientific conceptions into a moral and aesthetic framework. The author stresses that we will find this by experience rather than by explicit modern moralists translating scientific results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority should prefer humane letters over natural science in general education
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If there is to be separation and option between humane letters on the one hand, and the natural sciences on the other, the great majority of mankind... would do well, I cannot but think, to choose to be educated in humane letters rather than in the natural sciences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-specialists, humane letters call out more points of human being and better satisfy general human needs; thus curriculum choices for the many should prioritize letters, while allowing some scientific acquaintance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument-knowledges belong primarily to specialists; most need only limited schooling in them
rubrics_metrics.description: Some kinds of knowledge 'cannot be made to directly serve the instinct in question... These are instrument-knowledges; they lead on to other knowledges... A man who passes his life in instrument-knowledges is a specialist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat highly technical or formal subjects (e.g., deep mathematics, philological niceties) as instruments: valuable for those who can use them but not suitable as the main occupation for the majority. Provide some schooling in them, but avoid making them the dominant curriculum for general education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical education and Greek uniquely serve the instinct for beauty (symmetria prisca)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the instinct for beauty 'is served by Greek literature and art as it is served by no other literature and art,' we may trust humane instinct to keep Greek part of culture; Greek supplies the 'symmetria prisca'—a high symmetry combining details into a supreme total effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve and (where possible) expand rational study of Greek because its literature and art cultivate an essential aesthetic sense that other literatures do not replace. Use examples (Acropolis, architecture, Leonardo's quote) to argue for Greek's formative effect on taste and design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should familiarize students of letters with the general conceptions of modern science (and vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The student of humane letters only, will, at least, know also the great general conceptions brought in by modern physical science; but the student of the natural sciences only... will, by our very hypothesis, know nothing of humane letters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate a balanced awareness: those trained in letters should acquaint themselves with the chief results and conceptions of science, and everyone should receive as much scientific training 'as they can conveniently carry,' while preserving the central place of humane letters for most people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indiscriminate, promiscuous, or vapid reading; the misuse of books is debilitating
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'the misuse of books, the debilitating waste of brain in aimless, promiscuous, vapid reading, or even... the poisonous inhalation of mere literary garbage and bad men's worst thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the habit of consuming trivial or merely curious reading. Such reading 'closes our minds to what is solid and enlarging' and leads to ignorance of the greater literature. Actively exclude low-nutritive reading from one's regimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic reading: know what to read, in what order, with what connection, and what to exclude
rubrics_metrics.description: Faced with an 'immensity' of books, one needs 'judgment, method, discipline'—to decide 'what we should not read' and to keep 'that small cleared spot in the overgrown jungle of "information"' which is one's 'ordered patch of fruit-bearing knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a systematic program of reading (especially for self-educators and those guiding the young). Prioritize the enduring and indispensable books, create a connected course of study, and deliberately exclude much material to preserve depth over breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer not reading at all to saturating oneself with trivial books; form the habit of reading wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Of the two evils I prefer the former'—the author would rather a person not read at all than read promiscuously; 'the habit of reading idly debilitates and corrupts the mind... the habit of reading wisely is one of the most difficult habits to acquire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to form a disciplined, resolute habit of wise reading. Avoid maxims that encourage 'read anything to form a habit'—such a habit risks permanent debilitation. Invest 'infinite pains' and resolution to read with purpose and selectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturation with inferior books kills one's access to great books
rubrics_metrics.description: If we 'saturate our minds with the idler books, the "good book"... is dead to them: it is a book sealed up and buried.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reading time as scarce: overload with trivial literature and you lose the capacity to profit from classics and 'abiding parts of knowledge.' Make exclusionary choices to keep major works alive and usable.
